title: Writing in the Air

Lord George Murray and the Board of Admiralty

places: Admiralty Office, Whitehall/Charing Cross, London, and the line to Deal

Brûlon (sending end) and Parcé-sur-Sarthe (receiving end), about 15 km apart
Headquarters at Beaudignies, then Onnaing, before Le Quesnoy, Valenciennes and C

intro: On 2 March 1791, in the small Sarthe town of Brûlon, Claude Chappe and his brothers tried a strange thing in front of the town's officials. A panel, painted white on one side and black on the other, turned in step with a pendulum clock, and men about fifteen kilometres away at Parcé, watching through a telescope with a matching clock, wrote down a sentence they had not been told. The officials at both ends signed procès-verbaux, formal minutes, that the trial had worked. Three and a half years later the same family's arm-and-beam machines, standing on towers and church steeples from Lille to the Louvre, brought the National Convention news of a recaptured fortress while the deputies were still in session. This chapter follows that message in transit. It has almost no diaries. Its eyes are inventors' petitions and letters, municipal minutes, commissioners' reports, generals' dispatches, the printed proceedings of the Convention (the Archives parlementaires), London magazines and prints, and one memoir written thirty years later by Ignace Chappe, who sat in the Legislative Assembly and helped his brother. Each form tag says what kind of record it is. Most of the entries are what institutions wrote about a signal, not what a person felt, but they are exact to the hour in a way diaries seldom are. One example: a commissioner's report from July 1793 notes that the first signal was raised at twenty-six minutes past four. The political path ran through the Revolution's committees. Gilbert Romme reported on the invention to the Convention on 1 April 1793 and called it a way of writing in the air. Joseph Lakanal, Pierre Daunou and the mathematician Louis Arbogast watched a three-station trial north of Paris on 12 July 1793, and Lakanal's report of 25 July led the next day to Chappe's appointment as ingénieur télégraphe. The Committee of Public Safety, which ran the war, chose Lille, the base of the Army of the North, as the first line. The machine went into regular service in the summer of 1794, the same weeks in which Robespierre fell on 9 thermidor. The first messages of war were about the frontier fortresses held by the Austrians: Le Quesnoy, which surrendered on 28 thermidor an II (15 August 1794), and Condé, which gave up at six in the morning on 13 fructidor (30 August). The printed record does not support some of the later stories. Barère's report on Le Quesnoy came on 30 thermidor (17 August), and it said only that the news had reached Paris an hour after the garrison marched out. For Condé the proceedings are precise. Carnot read the telegraph's report 'just arrived', the Convention renamed the town Nord-Libre, and the decree went back up the line. At half past six that evening Chappe wrote that Lille had acknowledged receipt by telegraph. The whole exchange happened on a day the same assembly spent hearing Lecointre's charges against Barère, Billaud-Varenne and Collot d'Herbois. News of the device crossed the Channel within weeks. London magazin

title: What Hath God Wrought
eyes: The Baltimore Patriot and its Washington correspondent

intro: In 1837 three electric telegraphs appeared within months of one another. In London, William Fothergill Cooke and Charles Wheatstone patented a needle instrument in June. In Munich, Carl August Steinheil showed the Bavarian Academy a line that printed dots on paper tape in July. In New York, Samuel Morse, a painter turned professor, gave his first public demonstration in September and filed a caveat at the Patent Office that autumn. None of the three was yet news. The chapter follows how, over the next eight years, the wire stopped being a lecture-room curiosity and began to carry things people cared about: votes, nominations, and in January 1845 a description of a man wanted for murder. The American story is unusually well documented because it ran through Congress. Committee reports, the House vote of February 1843 and Morse's report of June 1844 to the Treasury are government records. Morse's letters to his brother Sidney, printed by his son in 1914, show the same months from inside: the waiting, the money running out, the quarrels on the construction gangs. Alfred Vail, who sat at the Baltimore end of the line, and Ezra Cornell, who built it, appear in their agreements, patents and later papers. Little of this is diary in the strict sense. The record is mostly dated letters, official reports, newspaper columns and court testimony, and the form tags say so. The heart of the chapter is the line between the Capitol in Washington and the Baltimore and Ohio depot in Baltimore in May 1844. On 1 May, before the line was finished, Vail sent the Whig ticket from Annapolis Junction about an hour ahead of the train. On 24 May came the message chosen by Annie Ellsworth, the young daughter of the Commissioner of Patents. Five days later the Democratic convention in Baltimore nominated Silas Wright, who was in the Senate in Washington, for vice-president. He declined by wire, and the delegates did not believe a machine could have brought his answer. In Britain the telegraph grew along the railways. Cooke and Wheatstone's line ran beside the Great Western from Paddington, and by 1843 it reached Slough. On the evening of 1 January 1845 a woman named Sarah Hart was found dying at Salt Hill near Slough. A description of the man seen leaving her house was telegraphed to Paddington ahead of his train. John Tawell was followed, arrested the next morning, tried at Aylesbury and hanged in March. The case is told here soberly, through the police and court record and the press. It made the telegraph famous in a way no demonstration had. Behind both stories runs a quarrel over credit. Joseph Henry at Princeton had shown in 1831 how to drive an electromagnet through a long wire, and he advised and endorsed Morse. When Vail's 1845 book left him out, the rift began. It ended in Morse's printed attack of 1855 and a Smithsonian Regents' report clearing Henry. In Britain, Cooke and Wheatstone went to arbitration in 1841 over who had invented what. These disputes are set out

intro: On the night of 4 August 1858 Cyrus Field rowed through the dark of Trinity Bay, Newfoundland, to a telegraph house where everyone was asleep. Behind him USS Niagara was paying out the last miles of a cable whose other end HMS Agamemnon was bringing into Valentia, on the far west coast of Ireland. For four weeks that summer a copper wire about 2,000 miles long carried messages between the Old World and the New. Then it went silent. Eight years, a government inquiry and the largest ship in the world were needed before the line worked to stay. This chapter follows messages rather than battles. The people who matter most are often those at the instruments: de Sauty at Bay Bulls Arm asking Ireland to send slower; Whitehouse at Valentia driving signals with induction coils; Thomson with his mirror galvanometer, a beam of light moving across a scale. The station logs, laid before the Joint Committee in 1860, show what the speeches left out. The Queen's greeting of about ninety-eight words took most of a night to get through, with a stop for repairs. The President's reply waited three days in Newfoundland. New York set its own City Hall alight celebrating a line that was already failing. Very little here is a diary in the strict sense. Field's journal survives as printed by his brother; Bright's diary as footnotes in a family biography; the 1858 traffic as a transcript and as tapes in the Kelvin Papers. The press, both New York's and The Times, appears as a collective eye. Whitehouse speaks through pamphlets written to defend himself. Canning, who ran the grapnels, left no diary that was consulted and is seen through others. The form tags say which is which. The second half belongs to the Great Eastern. W. H. Russell, the Times war correspondent, wrote up his daily diary of the 1865 voyage within months, with his assistant John Deane keeping a plainer diary beside him. Daniel Gooch, chairman of the ship's company and newly elected to Parliament, kept a true daily journal of both voyages. Their accounts of 2 August 1865, when the cable parted 600 miles from Newfoundland, can be laid minute against minute, though Gooch keeps ship's time and Russell Greenwich time. In July 1866 the new cable landed at Heart's Content. In September the grapnel brought up the lost 1865 cable from about two miles down and spliced it, and the operator at Valentia saw a signal from a line that had lain on the seabed for a year. The causes of 1858 are still argued. One position, the inquiry's and the standard one, blames Whitehouse's high voltages. Another stresses faults made in manufacture and in the laying machinery before he touched it. Both are set out here as positions.

title: Mr. Watson, Come Here: The Telephone and Its Rivals
places: Boston (5 Exeter Place lodgings and laboratory); Washington in Feb–Mar 1876; Phi
Boston, writing of a visit to Washington on 1 March
Cambridge and Boston; with Bell in England after July 1877
Cambridge, Massachusetts; directing the patent filing in Washington

Dominion Telegraph office, Robert White's shoe store, Paris, Ontario

intro: On a Monday in February 1876 two documents describing a way to send the human voice down a wire reached the United States Patent Office in Washington within hours of each other. One was Alexander Graham Bell's patent application, pushed through by his backer Gardiner Hubbard; the other was a caveat from Elisha Gray of Chicago. Four weeks later Bell held patent 174,465, and three days after that, in a Boston lodging house, his assistant Thomas Watson heard a sentence come out of the receiver. This chapter follows the message in transit at every scale: the first words passed between two rooms, Shakespeare recited to an emperor and a cable engineer at the Centennial Exhibition, songs sent one way over thirteen kilometres of Ontario telegraph wire, the first real two-way conversation across the Charles River, and finally a queen holding the tube to her ear at Osborne. Each call is laid against the notebook, letter or diary that recorded it. The other message in transit is the patent itself, and the paperwork about it. Who filed first, who saw what in the examiner's office, and whether Bell's crucial passage on variable resistance was there from the start were fought over for a decade. The record here is honest about its kind: Bell's laboratory notebook and letters are near-contemporary; Gray's letters were preserved as legal exhibits; Watson's lively memoir (1926) and the examiner Zenas Wilber's contradictory affidavits (1885 and 1886) are later, and are flagged as such. Positions are given with their evidence, not resolved. Around the two principals stand the rivals and witnesses: Thomas Edison at Menlo Park, whose carbon transmitter of 1877 made the telephone loud enough to use; Antonio Meucci on Staten Island, whose lapsed caveat of 1871 the US House of Representatives chose to honour in 2002; Dom Pedro II, whose own diary is cooler than the legend; and Mabel Hubbard, the deaf young woman to whom many of the inventor's letters were written. Two famous stories are flagged as legends: the 'My God, it talks!' exclamation, and the Western Union memo dismissing the telephone, which first appeared in 1968. Most of the record is letters, notebooks, legal papers and official actions rather than diaries in the strict sense; only the emperor and the queen kept true journals here. That mix is itself the point: an invention born in a patent race leaves its trace in documents written to be read by rivals, examiners and judges.

intro: Between 1894 and 1902 the invisible waves that Heinrich Hertz had produced in a laboratory became a way of sending messages across an ocean. Nobody did it alone, and almost nobody agreed afterwards on who did it first. This chapter lays the rival workers on one timeline: a Liverpool physicist lecturing in Oxford, a Bengali professor in Calcutta, a Russian navy teacher in St Petersburg, a young Italian with a patent agent in London, and German professors in Berlin and Strasbourg backed by an emperor. Their records are mostly not diaries. They are society papers, patent specifications, press reports, lecture transcripts and lawyers' letters, with two real pocket diaries at the centre: Marconi's terse one, with signal times in ink among pencil notes, and George Kemp's, kept by the assistant who hauled the apparatus onto islands and flew the kites. Kemp's diary exists in a brief contemporary form and a fuller typed version he made around 1930; the two are not always the same, and this chapter says which is meant where it can. The message in transit here is almost absurdly small: the Morse letter S, three dots, sent repeatedly from a great spark station at Poldhu in Cornwall and heard, on 12 December 1901, through a telephone earpiece on Signal Hill above St John's, Newfoundland. Only two men heard it, both from the same company, and nothing was written on tape. Within days a cable company's lawyers had ordered the experiment to stop, and engineers on both sides of the Atlantic were asking whether three dots were a signal or just static. The answer came at sea. In February 1902 Marconi sailed for New York on the SS Philadelphia and had the captain and chief officer sign the printed tapes as messages arrived from Poldhu: readable words to 1,551 miles, the letter S to 2,099. The same voyage revealed that signals carried much farther by night than by day, an effect no one had predicted. Priority runs under every entry. Lodge showed signals between buildings in 1894 but sent no message; Popov's 'Heinrich Hertz' telegram of 1896 rests on later recollection; Bose published openly and patented nothing, and his 1899 detector probably sat at Marconi's ear; Fleming built the sending station and felt erased from the story. These are set out here as positions with their evidence, not as verdicts.

intro: This chapter is a message log more than a set of diaries. On the night of 14–15 April 1912 almost everything that mattered about the Titanic passed through a few Marconi wireless rooms: six ice warnings during the day, the distress call after a quarter past midnight, the replies of ships too far away and the silence of one ship close by. The record that survives is made of station logs, message forms, sworn testimony and one survivor's book, and the forms are tagged honestly here. The sender is Jack Phillips, who died, and whose words survive only as other stations wrote them down and as his junior, Harold Bride, recalled them. The receivers are spread across the North Atlantic: Harold Cottam on the Carpathia, who answered by chance because he was still up; John Durrant on the Mount Temple, whose log, kept in New York time, gives the last hour almost minute by minute; Cyril Evans on the Californian, who had warned Titanic of ice and been told to keep out, and was asleep when she called for help; and the station at Cape Race, Newfoundland, which passed what it heard ashore. Ashore the message changed character. In New York the owners' office spent Monday repeating hopeful fragments, including reports that all were safe and the ship was in tow, until the Olympic's message arrived at 6.16 pm. The New York Times read meaning into silence and printed the worst. For three days the Carpathia's single operator gave priority to survivors' names, and on 18 April the two operators' stories were sold to the Times under an arrangement Marconi agreed to. Then came the questioners: Senator William Alden Smith, who opened hearings the day after the docking, and Lord Mersey's British inquiry, whose report set out which warnings reached the bridge and found that the Californian might have saved many if not all of the lives lost. Within months the United States required two operators and a constant watch on passenger ships and licensed every station; in January 1914 an international convention followed. (The US Radio Act is sometimes dated to 1913 because it took effect on 13 December 1912; it was signed on 13 August 1912.) About 1,500 people died. The chapter follows the operators and their messages and does not dwell on the deaths, but they are the reason every minute of the log was examined so closely. One famous story is left out of the facts: David Sarnoff's account, first published in 1926, of being first to hear the news and spending 72 hours at the key is a later legend and is flagged as such in the message log.

title: The Borrowed Wire
eyes: Venustiano Carranza (with Foreign Minister Cándido Aguilar)
places: German embassy, Washington; then at sea and back to Berlin

intro: On 16 January 1917 a long block of number groups left the German Foreign Office in Berlin. It was handed to the American embassy, which sent German diplomatic traffic over the State Department's own cable as a courtesy meant to help peace talks. The route ran through Copenhagen and London to Washington, where Ambassador Bernstorff was to pass the message to the German minister in Mexico City. In London, the Admiralty's codebreakers in Room 40 copied it as they copied everything on that cable. By the next morning Nigel de Grey and William Montgomery had a partial reading: unrestricted submarine war from 1 February and, if America came in, an alliance with Mexico, with Texas, New Mexico and Arizona as the prize and Japan invited to join. This chapter follows that message from sender to relay, interceptor, receivers and public. Bernstorff re-enciphered it and sent it on by Western Union. Admiral Hall held the decrypt for a month and then found a second copy in a Mexico City telegraph office. That copy let him hide that Britain was reading American cables. Balfour handed the text to Ambassador Page. Page's cable reached Wilson the same night. Lansing gave it to the Associated Press, and on 1 March it was on front pages across the country. Two days later Zimmermann confirmed it was genuine. The record here is mostly cables, letters and official memoranda rather than diaries, and the form tags say so. Page's cables, Lansing's and Polk's instructions, and Fletcher's reports from Mexico are printed in the State Department's Foreign Relations series, a US government record. Page's letters and diary notes were published in 1922. House's dictated diary is at Yale. The codebreakers' side survives as de Grey's manuscript worksheet and in accounts by de Grey and Hall written much later. Hall deliberately spread misleading stories about how the telegram was obtained, so those are given as positions. The Mexican and Japanese ends are told mostly through other people's reports. Carranza's answers survive as Fletcher heard them, as Eckardt reported them to Berlin, and in the formal reply of 14 April 1917. The two diplomats did not hear the same thing. Japan's denial is known from Foreign Minister Motono's newspaper interview, cabled by the American ambassador on the day Zimmermann admitted authorship. The message log sets out the timings: Page's cable leaving London at 1 p.m. and arriving at 8:30 p.m. Washington time, Fletcher's replies arriving before dawn, and Tokyo's denial crossing the Pacific overnight. The plan never came close to working. But its interception, the decision to reveal it, the cover story and the publication show nearly every part of signals intelligence that would follow: intercept, decrypt, protecting the source, verification and press management.

title: AF Is Short of Water: The Signals Behind Midway
eyes: Cyril Thomas Simard (Naval Air Station Midway)
places: About 700 miles west of Midway, bearing 261
Battleship Yamato, several hundred miles behind the carriers

intro: In the spring of 1942 the Imperial Japanese Navy planned to seize Midway Atoll and draw the remaining American carriers into a decisive battle. Its orders went out by radio in the fleet's main code, JN-25(b), and three Allied listening stations, at Pearl Harbor, Melbourne and Washington, were by then reading fragments of it. This chapter follows those messages, and the bait and contact reports that answered them, from March to the aftermath in October. Most of the record here is not diaries. It is intelligence summaries, dispatches, radio contact reports, a commander's running estimate and action report, a Japanese battle report captured and translated by the US Navy, and newspaper and grand-jury records. Only Ugaki Matome's diary is a diary in the strict sense. Several of the best-known stories, including the water ruse, Layton's forecast and Fuchida's account of the carriers' last minutes, come from memoirs written long afterward, and they are flagged as such. The heart of the chapter is a set of arguments over messages. Was AF Midway, as Pearl Harbor and Melbourne said, or might it be somewhere else, as voices in Washington suggested? Would the attack come in early June or later? Who first broke the cipher that encoded the date? The record gives positions with evidence, and where NSA's own histories disagree, both are shown. On 3 and 4 June the messages became contact reports. American patrol planes from Midway reported the occupation force, then the carriers, in short coded signals. A Japanese float plane launched late from the cruiser Tone found the American fleet and reported it imprecisely, while its own commanders' questions were overheard. The difference between those two sets of signals is part of how four Japanese carriers were lost. The battle killed about 307 Americans and more than 3,000 Japanese, many of them aircraft mechanics below decks. The chapter records those losses without detail and then follows the secret into its afterlife: a Chicago newspaper that printed what amounted to a decrypt, a grand jury that declined to indict, and the transfer of the codebreaker whose unit had done most of the work.

intro: Between 1960 and 1970 the idea of chopping messages into small blocks and letting computers pass them from switch to switch went from a Cold War survivability study to a working network. It did not have a single inventor. Paul Baran at RAND in Santa Monica and Donald Davies at the National Physical Laboratory outside London reached the same design separately, for different reasons, and neither built it first. The American network came out of ARPA's Information Processing Techniques Office, where Bob Taylor wanted his agency's computers linked and Larry Roberts drew up the plan. In October 1967, at a symposium in Gatlinburg, Tennessee, a British engineer, Roger Scantlebury, explained packets to Roberts and pointed him to Baran's unread reports. A year later Bolt Beranek and Newman in Cambridge won the contract to build the switches, the Interface Message Processors, and a senator's congratulatory telegram got the name wrong. The record here is mostly not diaries. It is dated reports and memoranda (RAND's, NPL's, BBN's quarterly reports to ARPA), the Request for Comments series that graduate students began in April 1969, one handwritten log book at UCLA, and a great deal of later recollection. Where a date or detail rests only on recollection, the entry says so. The centre of the chapter is one evening: Wednesday 29 October 1969, about 22:30 Pacific Standard Time. Charley Kline at UCLA tried to log in to Bill Duvall's computer at SRI, 350 miles north, the two of them talking on the telephone as each letter went. Two letters arrived before the system crashed. The log records it in one line, and the later accounts disagree on details. Who invented packet switching is still argued. Baran and Davies are credited by most historians with independent invention; Leonard Kleinrock, whose 1961–64 queueing work analysed message-switched networks, has since the 1990s claimed to have laid its theoretical foundation, and Davies, Taylor and others have rejected that. The chapter sets out the positions and the evidence and leaves the verdict to the reader. A short coda follows the network to its first email in 1971, its public demonstration in Washington in October 1972, and the French CYCLADES network whose ideas fed the internet's protocols.
